title: Size of the Jenkins band, inaugural parades and bands White heard around the country
summary: White describes band strength, the inaugural parades of 1904, 1908 and 1912, Edmund Jenkins, and the Black bands he met in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and elsewhere.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: This band also was playing on the Midway at the Buffalo Exposition in 1902. I was not a member of it then. The band under the direction of P.M. Logan, we call him Hotze for a nickname. Professor P.M. Logan, a marvelous musician.
How big is the band? You never mentioned how big it is.

Oh, nothing under 30 pieces. Nothing under 30 pieces at no time. Mr. Jenkins kept it up at that strength for years. In the winter in Florida, when they take the tour down in Florida for the winter season, then it would drill down to say about 20, some odd, maybe 24. Because the bigger boys in the band, the larger and more older boys, they kept them in school. Because he would always stress an education. So the boys who were members of the band, ranging in age from 12 to 16, he put them in the classroom so they could further their education. He'd take the young ones down in Florida. And Mr. P.G. Degas, who is now president of the home now, was always accompanying this band wherever they went. You see, he is the nephew of Mr. Jenkins. And he now, he succeeded to the pastor of the Fourth Baptist Church in Charleston. He's presently there now, if he hasn't passed at this time. Last I heard of it, and that was just about a year or so ago, he was actively heading the institution. This band played inaugural parades for Theodore Roosevelt. I happened to be in that one, 1904. I'm almost 15 now. In 1908, when William Howard Taft was elected president, this band was also in there. That parade. I was in that band. In 1912, for Woodrow Wilson, the Democrats came to power and the Democrats in South Carolina didn't want the Jenkins-Ownage band to appear in this inauguration parade. But the staunch Republicans from upstate saw that the band went just the same. They paid the expenses. Now, there is no other record of any small, uh, kid, Negro band having these honors. Then they went from there to the London stadium. And that was, uh, last year, uh, I served with the band. Because I was already a student in Benedict College in 1900, latter part of 10 and 11. But I, I went with the band East that summer as director of the band. And Mr. Jenkins' son, Edmund, who had won seven consecutive scholarships for clarinet manipulation, violin, piano, and the theory of music, was back, uh, and he took charge of the band. It's quite an honor to have the son of the president directed the band. And he was, he could also play skillfully these, uh, very, very articulate solos on the clarinet, on the pipe organ, he would speak, dance just as accurately as his fingers did almost. And he was called the Black Prodigy of Europe. Incidentally, I might mention here that some things written about music come from people who know nothing about it. In my travels around the country, I had the pleasure of meeting great Negro bands in Tampa, Florida, Key West, the Shackleford family there, Jacksonville, Florida, uh, Willie Lewis, whose son now is a marvelous musician in New York, led the Welcome Cornette band, they called it. There were two bands in Jacksonville, but I'll tell you about that a little later. There were marvelous bands in Savannah and Atlanta. I might mention that, uh, Miller's band in Savannah was well uniformed, well tutored, and played very good. Uh, we had no outstanding bands in South Carolina except the Jenkins orphanage band of Charleston and Tom Pinckney's band of Columbia, South Carolina. While I was a student at Benedict, I played in Tom Pinckney's band. Hardy, who was one of my teachers in my early days in the orphanage, had taken charge of Pinckney's band in Columbia and Hardy put me in the band. So while I was a student at Benedict, I still served in Pinckney's band on occasions. I could name to you several fine bands in America that we had come up against that we had the pleasure of hearing because we were widely traveled, such as Bill Berry's band of St. Louis, Missouri, a band of 50 pieces, whom I heard in concert in New York in 1908. And then Bill went on to Illinois to take charge of the 8th Regiment band, and I heard Bill's band again. So in my travels around the country, I had a chance to hear a little more than the ordinary fellow could hear from staying at home. Even down in Pensacola, Florida down there, they had a wonderful band down there, the Weyer family. Old Man Weyer himself directed the band, and one of the greatest violinists in America, Paul Weyer, is a product of that band. Now the bands down in Pensacola in the lower south never numbered more than 10, hardly more than 15 pieces. They thought they had a heck of a fine band when they had as many as 15 pieces. But no band in the whole United States, nowhere in the world, topped the Jenkins band of Charleston,
South Carolina, and that's the band I came up in. How young were the youngest ones in there usually?
